title: The skull: vault, face and sutures
summary: Twenty-two bones, but only eight of them enclose the brain — learn those first.
objectives: Name the eight bones of the neurocranium and point to each on the model
Trace the coronal, sagittal and lambdoid sutures and say which bones each separates
Explain why the pterion is the most dangerous point on the side of the head
Relate the hard palate and nasal septum to the bones that form them
takeaways: Neurocranium = frontal, two parietal, two temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid.
The pterion is where four bones meet over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.
Sutures are fibrous joints: they allow growth, not movement, and fuse with age.
Maxillae and palatine bones form the hard palate; the bony nasal septum is mainly ethmoid and vomer.

steps.title: The whole skull first
steps.text:
The skull divides into the neurocranium, the box that holds the brain, and the viscerocranium, the face hung on the front of it. Eight bones make the box: the frontal, two parietals, two temporals, the occipital, the sphenoid and the ethmoid.

Everything else — maxillae, zygomatics, nasal bones, mandible and the small bones inside the nose — is face. Spin the model and pick the boundary out for yourself: the face stops where the frontal bone begins.

check.q: How many bones make up the neurocranium, and which of them is unpaired but sits deepest?
check.a: Eight. The sphenoid is unpaired and sits deepest, wedged across the base between the face and the brain.

steps.title: The vault from above
steps.text:
Looking down on the vault you see three sutures. The coronal suture runs across the top between the frontal bone and the two parietals. The sagittal suture runs front to back between the parietals. The lambdoid suture separates the parietals from the occipital behind.

Where coronal meets sagittal is the bregma — the anterior fontanelle in an infant, which stays open until about eighteen months and is the window a paediatrician feels for dehydration or raised pressure. Where sagittal meets lambdoid is the lambda.
steps.mnemonic: The sutures are named for their shapes: a crown (coronal), an arrow (sagittal), a Greek lambda.

check.q: Which fontanelle lies at the bregma and when does it close?
check.a: The anterior fontanelle, between frontal and parietal bones. It closes at about 18 months.

steps.title: The temporal bone and the pterion
steps.text:
Turn to the side. The temporal bone is the busiest bone in the body: it carries the ear apparatus, the mastoid air cells, the styloid process, the mandibular fossa and the carotid canal.

Just above the zygomatic arch, four bones meet at the pterion: frontal, parietal, temporal and the greater wing of the sphenoid. The bone here is thin, and the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on its inner surface. A blow that cracks the pterion tears the artery and produces an extradural haematoma — the classic lucid interval, then rapid deterioration.
steps.clinical: An extradural bleed is arterial and fast; a subdural is venous, from bridging veins, and can take days to declare itself.

check.q: Which four bones meet at the pterion, and what lies deep to it?
check.a: Frontal, parietal, temporal and the greater wing of the sphenoid — over the anterior branch of the middle meningeal artery.

steps.title: The face
steps.text:
The face is built round the two maxillae, which carry the upper teeth, form the floor of the orbit, the floor of the nose and most of the hard palate, and are hollowed out by the maxillary sinuses.

The zygomatic bone makes the cheek prominence and, with the temporal bone, the zygomatic arch. The nasal bones make only the bridge; the rest of the nose is cartilage. The mandible is the only bone of the skull that moves.
steps.pitfall: The hard palate is made by two bones, not one: the palatine processes of the maxillae in front and the horizontal plates of the palatine bones behind. A cleft can involve either or both.

steps.title: The ethmoid, hidden in the middle
steps.text:
The ethmoid is a small, delicate box you cannot see from outside. It roofs the nasal cavity, makes the medial wall of each orbit, carries the superior and middle conchae and holds the cribriform plate, through which the olfactory nerves pass.

Two consequences follow from how thin it is. A blow to the face can fracture the cribriform plate and let CSF leak into the nose (rhinorrhoea), an open door for meningitis. And the lamina papyracea — literally 'paper layer' — is so thin that infection in the ethmoid sinuses spreads straight into the orbit.
steps.clinical: Orbital cellulitis in a child is usually ethmoid sinusitis that has crossed the lamina papyracea.

check.q: Clear fluid drips from the nose of a patient after facial trauma. What has probably broken?
check.a: The cribriform plate of the ethmoid, letting CSF into the nasal cavity.

steps.title: A roof below and a partition above
steps.text:
Look at the maxillae and picture their horizontal shelves meeting in the midline. These palatine processes make the anterior part of the hard palate; the horizontal plates of the palatine bones complete it behind. The same shelf is the roof of the mouth and the floor of the nose.

Above it, the bony nasal septum is formed mainly by the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid superiorly and the vomer posteroinferiorly. Septal cartilage continues it forwards. Separate the two ideas: the palate divides mouth from nose, while the septum divides the two nasal cavities.

check.q: Which partition separates the mouth from the nose, and which separates right from left within the nose?
check.a: The palate separates mouth from nose; the nasal septum separates the right and left nasal cavities.

steps.pitfall: The external nasal bones form the bridge of the nose, not most of its internal septum.

title: The floor of the skull and what leaves by each hole
summary: Three fossae, a dozen foramina, and a way to remember which nerve uses which.
objectives: Divide the skull base into anterior, middle and posterior fossae and say what sits in each
State the contents of the major foramina
Predict the deficit from a fracture through a given part of the base
Distinguish a nerve entering a bony canal from its final exit from the skull
takeaways: Anterior fossa: frontal lobes. Middle: temporal lobes and pituitary. Posterior: cerebellum and brainstem.
Superior orbital fissure carries III, IV, V1 and VI — everything that moves the eye, plus its sensation.
Foramen magnum transmits the medulla, the vertebral arteries and the spinal accessory nerve going up.
VII enters the temporal bone with VIII at the internal acoustic meatus, but exits through the stylomastoid foramen.

steps.title: Three steps down
steps.text:
Cut the skull across and look into it from above. The floor descends in three terraces. The anterior cranial fossa, shallowest, holds the frontal lobes and the olfactory bulbs. The middle cranial fossa, shaped like a butterfly, holds the temporal lobes with the pituitary in the middle. The posterior cranial fossa, deepest, holds the cerebellum and the brainstem.

Nearly every cranial nerve leaves through this floor, and the fossa tells you roughly which: I in the anterior, II to VI in the middle, VII to XII in the posterior.

check.q: Which fossa holds the pituitary gland?
check.a: The middle cranial fossa, in the hypophysial fossa of the sella turcica of the sphenoid.

steps.title: The anterior fossa and the olfactory route
steps.text:
The floor here is the orbital plate of the frontal bone with the cribriform plate of the ethmoid in the middle and the lesser wings of the sphenoid behind.

Only one thing passes: the olfactory nerve filaments, twenty or so on each side, running up from the nasal mucosa to the olfactory bulb sitting on the plate. Shearing at this level in a head injury is the commonest cause of anosmia after trauma.

steps.title: The middle fossa: the busy floor
steps.text:
Work back to front through the greater wing of the sphenoid.

The optic canal carries the optic nerve and the ophthalmic artery. The superior orbital fissure carries the oculomotor (III), trochlear (IV), ophthalmic (V1) and abducens (VI) nerves, plus the ophthalmic veins. Foramen rotundum takes the maxillary nerve (V2), foramen ovale the mandibular nerve (V3), and foramen spinosum, just behind it, the middle meningeal artery.
steps.mnemonic: Standing Room Only: Superior orbital fissure, Rotundum, Ovale — front to back, and V1, V2, V3 in the same order.

check.q: A patient cannot abduct the right eye and has numbness of the forehead. Where is the lesion?
check.a: The right superior orbital fissure or cavernous sinus — VI and V1 together.

steps.title: The posterior fossa
steps.text:
The internal acoustic meatus in the petrous temporal bone takes the facial (VII) and vestibulocochlear (VIII) nerves. The jugular foramen takes IX, X and XI out, and the internal jugular vein with them. The hypoglossal canal takes XII.

The foramen magnum is the exit for the medulla as it becomes the spinal cord, and the entrance for the vertebral arteries and the spinal roots of the accessory nerve. Because the posterior fossa is a rigid box with only this one big hole, a swelling here forces the cerebellar tonsils down through it — coning.
steps.clinical: A vestibular schwannoma grows in the internal acoustic meatus: deafness and tinnitus first, then facial weakness as it presses on VII.

steps.title: Base of skull fracture
steps.text:
Now put it to use. A fracture through the anterior fossa gives periorbital bruising with no other injury to the eye — raccoon eyes — and CSF rhinorrhoea.

A fracture through the petrous temporal bone gives blood behind the eardrum, CSF otorrhoea, bruising over the mastoid (Battle's sign) and often a facial palsy, because the facial nerve runs through that bone in its own canal.

check.q: Bruising over the mastoid with clear fluid from the ear. Which bone is fractured, and which cranial nerve is at risk?
check.a: The petrous part of the temporal bone; the facial nerve (VII) runs through it.

steps.title: An entrance is not always an exit
steps.text:
Follow the facial nerve into the petrous temporal bone. The internal acoustic meatus is an entrance to a passage through the bone, not VII's final opening onto the face. The nerve travels in the facial canal before emerging through the stylomastoid foramen. VIII stays with the hearing and balance apparatus.

This extra journey explains why the level of a facial nerve injury matters. A lesion within the temporal bone can affect branches for taste, stapedius or lacrimation, depending on its position. An injury after the stylomastoid foramen mainly affects the muscles of facial expression. Identify the temporal bone, then describe these two openings without treating them as interchangeable.

check.q: Why can an injury inside the temporal bone cause more than facial muscle weakness?
check.a: Branches for functions such as taste, stapedius and lacrimation leave VII before its final exit; a sufficiently proximal lesion can interrupt them too.

title: What makes a vertebra typical, and the four that are not
summary: One plan repeated 24 times, modified for the load each region carries.
objectives: Name the parts of a typical vertebra
Tell a cervical, thoracic and lumbar vertebra apart at a glance
Explain how C1 and C2 are built for rotation rather than weight
Explain how discs and paired facet joints share movement between adjacent vertebrae
takeaways: Cervical: small body, foramen transversarium, bifid spine. Thoracic: costal facets. Lumbar: massive kidney-shaped body.
The atlas has no body — it gave it to the axis as the dens.
Roughly half of all neck rotation happens at the atlanto-axial joint alone.
A motion segment includes a disc between vertebral bodies and two synovial facet joints behind; no disc lies between C1 and C2.

steps.title: The whole column
steps.text:
Twenty-four mobile vertebrae, then the fused sacrum and coccyx: 7 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar. The curves alternate — cervical and lumbar convex forwards (lordosis), thoracic and sacral convex backwards (kyphosis).

The thoracic and sacral curves are primary: the fetus has them in the womb. The cervical curve appears when a baby lifts its head, and the lumbar curve when it stands. Curves let the column act like a spring instead of a pillar.

check.q: Which two curves are present at birth?
check.a: The thoracic and sacral curves — the primary curves.

steps.title: The typical vertebra
steps.text:
In front, a weight-bearing body. Behind it, a ring — two pedicles and two laminae — enclosing the vertebral foramen, through which the spinal cord passes. Off the ring: a spinous process behind, two transverse processes sideways, and four articular processes, two up and two down, which meet the neighbours at the facet joints.

Between consecutive pedicles is the intervertebral foramen, where the spinal nerve leaves. Anything that narrows it — a disc bulge, an osteophyte, a collapsed body — presses the nerve.

check.q: Which two parts of the bony ring form the roof of the vertebral canal?
check.a: The two laminae, meeting in the midline at the base of the spinous process.

steps.title: Cervical: light, and drilled for arteries
steps.text:
A cervical vertebra has a small, wide body and — the giveaway — a foramen transversarium in each transverse process. The vertebral artery climbs through those foramina from C6 to C1 before turning into the skull.

The spinous processes of C3–C6 are short and bifid. C7 has a long, single spine you can feel at the base of the neck: the vertebra prominens, and the landmark from which you count ribs and place a chest drain.
steps.pitfall: The vertebral artery enters at C6, not C7 — the foramen transversarium of C7 usually carries only a small vein.

steps.title: Atlas and axis
steps.text:
The top two are built for the head to nod and swivel on. The atlas (C1) is a ring with no body at all: two lateral masses joined by an anterior and a posterior arch. Its cupped superior facets take the occipital condyles, and that joint is where you nod — 'yes'.

The axis (C2) carries the dens, a peg projecting up into the ring of the atlas, held against its anterior arch by the transverse ligament. The atlas and the head rotate around it — 'no'. About half of all cervical rotation happens here.
steps.clinical: In rheumatoid arthritis the transverse ligament can erode: the atlas slips forwards on the axis and the dens threatens the cord. Anaesthetists ask about neck symptoms before intubating for exactly this reason.

check.q: Where do you nod, and where do you shake your head?
check.a: Nodding at the atlanto-occipital joint; shaking at the atlanto-axial joint around the dens.

steps.title: Thoracic and lumbar
steps.text:
A thoracic vertebra is recognised by its costal facets — demifacets on the body for the head of a rib, and a facet on the transverse process for the rib's tubercle. Its spinous process points steeply downwards, overlapping the one below like roof tiles, and its facet joints lie in the coronal plane, which allows rotation but little flexion.

A lumbar vertebra has a massive kidney-shaped body, a short blunt spinous process, and facet joints in the sagittal plane, which allow flexion and extension but almost no rotation. Force a rotation and it is the disc that suffers.

check.q: Why does the thoracic spine rotate well and the lumbar spine badly?
check.a: The plane of the facet joints: coronal in the thorax, sagittal in the lumbar spine.

steps.title: Holding it together
steps.text:
Down the front of the bodies runs the broad anterior longitudinal ligament, which resists extension. Down the back of them, inside the canal, is the narrower posterior longitudinal ligament. Because it narrows as it descends, a lumbar disc usually herniates posterolaterally, where the ligament does not cover it — straight onto the nerve root.

Behind, the ligamenta flava join lamina to lamina, and the supraspinous and interspinous ligaments join the tips of the spines. A lumbar puncture needle passes through skin, fat, supraspinous and interspinous ligaments, then ligamentum flavum, and finally dura.

check.q: Which ligament gives the characteristic 'give' as an epidural needle passes it?
check.a: The ligamentum flavum — loss of resistance immediately after it marks the epidural space.

steps.title: Three joints for one moving segment
steps.text:
Two neighbouring typical vertebrae meet in three places: at the disc between their bodies and at a pair of facet joints behind. The disc is a fibrocartilaginous symphysis; each facet joint is synovial. The front carries and cushions load while the back guides the direction of movement.

The annulus fibrosus is the disc's layered outer ring and the nucleus pulposus its water-rich centre. Compression spreads force through the nucleus into the annulus and vertebral endplates. Compare that arrangement with atlas and axis: there is no intervertebral disc between C1 and C2, where the dens provides a pivot instead.

check.q: What are the three joints in a typical vertebral motion segment?
check.a: One intervertebral symphysis through the disc and two synovial facet joints.

title: The thoracic cage
summary: Twelve ribs, a three-part sternum and one angle you can feel that tells you where you are.
objectives: Distinguish true, false and floating ribs
Use the sternal angle to locate six things at once
Describe the parts of a typical rib and where a fracture is dangerous
Distinguish the superior thoracic aperture from the diaphragm-covered inferior aperture
takeaways: Ribs 1–7 true, 8–10 false, 11–12 floating.
The sternal angle is level with T4/5, the second costal cartilage, the carina and the start and end of the aortic arch.
The neurovascular bundle runs in the costal groove at the lower border, so a chest drain goes just above a rib.
The superior aperture connects neck and thorax; the larger inferior aperture is closed by the diaphragm.

steps.title: The cage as a whole
steps.text:
The thoracic cage protects the heart and lungs, gives the muscles of respiration something to pull on, and supports the shoulder girdle. Twelve pairs of ribs run from the thoracic vertebrae behind, down and forwards to the sternum in front — every rib slopes downwards, which is what allows the 'pump handle' and 'bucket handle' movements of breathing.

Ribs 1–7 reach the sternum by their own costal cartilage: true ribs. Ribs 8–10 join the cartilage above instead: false ribs. Ribs 11 and 12 end in the abdominal wall muscle: floating ribs.

check.q: Which ribs are 'false' and why?
check.a: 8, 9 and 10 — their cartilages join the cartilage above rather than the sternum directly.

steps.title: A typical rib
steps.text:
Follow one round. At the back it has a head with two facets, which meets the body of its own vertebra and the one above; a neck; and a tubercle, which meets the transverse process. Then the shaft turns sharply forwards at the angle and runs round to its cartilage.

Along the inner surface of the lower border is the costal groove, and in it lie the intercostal vein, artery and nerve — VAN, from the top down. That is why you aim for the upper border of the rib below when you put a needle into the chest.
steps.mnemonic: VAN from above down in the costal groove: Vein, Artery, Nerve.

check.q: You are draining a pleural effusion. Do you go above or below the rib, and why?
check.a: Above the lower rib — the neurovascular bundle hugs the groove under the rib above.

steps.title: The sternum and the angle of Louis
steps.text:
Three parts: the manubrium, the body, and the small xiphoid process. Manubrium and body meet at a palpable ridge, the sternal angle (angle of Louis), and this is the single most useful landmark in the chest.

At that level you find: the second costal cartilage (so you count ribs from there), the disc between T4 and T5, the carina where the trachea divides, the beginning and end of the arch of the aorta, and the upper limit of the pericardium.

check.q: Name three structures at the level of the sternal angle.
check.a: Second costal cartilage, T4/5 disc, carina, start and end of the aortic arch — any three.

steps.title: The first rib is not typical
steps.text:
The first rib is short, flat and sharply curved, and it lies almost horizontally. On its upper surface, the scalene tubercle separates two grooves: the subclavian vein in front of it, the subclavian artery and the lower trunk of the brachial plexus behind.

Everything leaving the neck for the arm must cross this rib, which makes it the floor of the thoracic outlet. A cervical rib — an extra rib from C7 — squeezes the same passage and can produce hand wasting or a cold, pulseless arm.
steps.clinical: A fractured first rib takes real force and should make you look for injury to the great vessels behind it.

steps.title: Fractures, flail and the protected organs
steps.text:
Ribs 4–9 break most often, usually at the angle where they are weakest. Three or more consecutive ribs broken in two places gives a flail segment that moves paradoxically — in on inspiration — and the real danger is the lung bruised beneath it.

The lowest ribs matter for what they cover: the liver on the right, the spleen on the left, and the kidneys behind. A fracture of ribs 9–11 on the left should always raise the question of a splenic tear.

check.q: Fractures of the left ninth to eleventh ribs. Which organ do you worry about?
check.a: The spleen.

steps.title: The two openings of the cage
steps.text:
The cage has an opening at each end. The superior thoracic aperture is bounded by T1 behind, the first ribs and their cartilages at the sides, and the upper border of the manubrium in front. It is the crowded connection between the neck and the chest.

The inferior aperture is much larger: T12 behind, ribs 11 and 12 posterolaterally, the costal margins and the xiphisternal region in front. The diaphragm attaches around this opening and domes above it. Its height explains how upper abdominal organs can lie behind lower ribs without being in the thoracic cavity.

check.q: Why can a lower rib overlie the liver even though the liver is an abdominal organ?
check.a: The diaphragm domes above the inferior thoracic aperture, so part of the abdomen lies inside the lower rib cage.

title: The pectoral girdle: clavicle and scapula
summary: The arm is attached to the trunk by one small joint, and that is the whole design.
objectives: Name the only bony joint between the upper limb and the axial skeleton
Identify the parts of the scapula and the muscles that use them
Explain the displacement of a fractured clavicle
Trace force from the hand to the trunk through the shoulder girdle
takeaways: The sternoclavicular joint is the only bone-to-bone link between arm and trunk.
The clavicle is the most commonly fractured bone in the body, usually at the middle third.
Scapular movement contributes about a third of total shoulder elevation.
The clavicle acts as a strut; force reaches the axial skeleton through the sternoclavicular joint.

steps.title: One joint holds the arm on
steps.text:
Look at the girdle from the front. The clavicle runs from the manubrium to the acromion, and the sternoclavicular joint at its medial end is the only place where the upper limb is bolted to the axial skeleton. Everything else — the scapula and all it carries — is slung on muscle.

That is the trade the shoulder makes. Almost no bony constraint means a huge range of movement, and a permanent liability to dislocation and to muscular fatigue.

check.q: What is the only bony articulation between the upper limb and the axial skeleton?
check.a: The sternoclavicular joint.

steps.title: The clavicle, and why it breaks where it does
steps.text:
The clavicle is S-shaped: convex forwards medially, concave forwards laterally. The junction of those two curves, at the middle third, is its weakest point and where about 80% of fractures happen — usually from a fall onto the shoulder.

The fragments then move in a predictable way. Sternocleidomastoid pulls the medial fragment up; the weight of the arm and pectoralis major pull the lateral fragment down and medially. Underneath run the subclavian vessels and the brachial plexus, which is what makes the injury worth examining properly.
steps.pitfall: In a child the same fall gives a greenstick clavicle fracture or a pulled elbow, not a dislocation — their ligaments are stronger than their bones.

steps.title: The scapula from behind
steps.text:
A flat triangle lying on ribs 2 to 7. The spine divides its back into the supraspinous and infraspinous fossae and runs laterally into the acromion, the bony point of the shoulder.

Learn three borders (superior, medial, lateral), three angles (superior, inferior, lateral) and three processes (spine, acromion, coracoid). Almost every muscle acting on the shoulder attaches to one of them, so the landmarks are worth the effort.

steps.title: The glenoid and the coracoid
steps.text:
Turn to the lateral angle. The glenoid fossa is a shallow, pear-shaped socket — about a third of the humeral head touches it at any moment, deepened only a little by the fibrocartilaginous labrum. Above and below it, the supraglenoid and infraglenoid tubercles give origin to the long heads of biceps and triceps.

The coracoid process hooks forwards like a bent finger. Three structures hang from it: pectoralis minor, the short head of biceps and coracobrachialis, and it is the anchor for the coracoclavicular ligaments that really hold the clavicle down.

check.q: Why does a torn acromioclavicular joint capsule alone not give a badly dropped shoulder?
check.a: The coracoclavicular ligaments are the real suspensory ligaments; the shoulder only drops badly when they tear too.

steps.title: Scapulohumeral rhythm
steps.text:
Raising the arm above the head is not a single joint's work. For roughly every two degrees at the glenohumeral joint, the scapula rotates one degree on the chest wall — the 2:1 scapulohumeral rhythm. Of 180° of elevation, about 60° belongs to the scapula.

The scapula is rotated by trapezius and serratus anterior working as a force couple. Paralyse serratus anterior (long thoracic nerve) and the scapula wings and the arm cannot be raised fully — a neat demonstration that the girdle is part of the shoulder.

check.q: Which nerve, when injured, causes a winged scapula?
check.a: The long thoracic nerve, supplying serratus anterior.

steps.title: Follow a push back to the chest
steps.text:
Imagine pushing against a wall. Force travels from the hand through the forearm and humerus to the scapula. From there the acromioclavicular connection and the strong coracoclavicular ligaments couple the scapula to the clavicle. The clavicle carries the force towards the sternum.

The clavicle also acts as a strut, holding the shoulder laterally so the arm can move clear of the chest. Its sternoclavicular joint must allow elevation, protraction and rotation as the arm rises. A moving shoulder therefore needs a moving clavicle, even when attention is fixed on the humeral head.

check.q: Which joint is the last bony link in the route from the hand to the axial skeleton?
check.a: The sternoclavicular joint, between the clavicle and the manubrium.

title: Humerus, radius and ulna
summary: Three bones and four nerves that run so close to them that the fracture tells you the deficit.
objectives: Name the parts of the humerus and the nerve related to each
Explain why the radius, not the ulna, carries the hand
Predict the nerve injury from a given fracture level
Describe how the interosseous membrane shares load between radius and ulna
takeaways: Surgical neck → axillary nerve. Radial groove → radial nerve. Medial epicondyle → ulnar nerve. Supracondylar → median nerve and brachial artery.
The radius carries the hand; the ulna carries the elbow.
Pronation and supination are the radius rotating over a stationary ulna.
The interosseous membrane transfers part of the load from the radius at the wrist towards the ulna proximally.

steps.title: The humerus, top to bottom
steps.text:
The head faces medially, backwards and up into the glenoid. Below it the anatomical neck, then the greater and lesser tubercles with the intertubercular groove between them holding the tendon of the long head of biceps.

The surgical neck is where the bone narrows below the tubercles — and where it breaks. The axillary nerve and the posterior circumflex humeral vessels wind round it, so test the badge patch of skin over the deltoid before and after you reduce one.

check.q: Which nerve is at risk in a surgical neck fracture, and how do you test it quickly?
check.a: The axillary nerve — sensation over the deltoid 'regimental badge' area and attempted abduction.

steps.title: The shaft and the radial groove
steps.text:
The shaft carries the deltoid tuberosity on its lateral side. Spiralling down the back of the shaft is the radial groove, and in it the radial nerve with the profunda brachii artery.

A mid-shaft fracture, or a long night asleep with the arm over the back of a chair ('Saturday night palsy'), damages the nerve here. The result is wrist drop: the extensors of wrist and fingers are paralysed while the elbow flexors, supplied higher up, are spared.
steps.clinical: Triceps is usually spared in a mid-shaft injury because its branches leave the nerve above the groove.

steps.title: The lower end and the supracondylar fracture
steps.text:
The lower humerus flares into two epicondyles with two articular surfaces between them: the capitulum laterally for the radial head, and the trochlea medially for the trochlear notch of the ulna.

The medial epicondyle has the ulnar nerve in a groove behind it — the 'funny bone'. Just above them, the bone is thin from front to back: this is where a child falling on an outstretched hand sustains a supracondylar fracture, and where the brachial artery and median nerve lie directly against the bone.
steps.clinical: The feared complication of a supracondylar fracture is Volkmann's ischaemic contracture: a compromised brachial artery, a swollen forearm and, hours later, dead muscle.

check.q: Which nerve lies behind the medial epicondyle?
check.a: The ulnar nerve.

steps.title: Radius and ulna: which carries what
steps.text:
At the elbow the ulna does the work: its olecranon and trochlear notch grip the trochlea of the humerus like a spanner, and that is the hinge. At the wrist the radius does the work: the ulna does not reach the carpus, and the hand hangs from the radius across a triangular fibrocartilage.

So the ulna carries the elbow and the radius carries the hand. That is why a fall on the outstretched hand fractures the distal radius, and why a displaced radial fracture ruins grip.

check.q: Which forearm bone articulates with the carpus?
check.a: The radius; the ulna is separated from the carpus by the triangular fibrocartilage.

steps.title: Pronation and supination
steps.text:
Turning the palm over is the radius rolling across a stationary ulna, pivoting at the proximal and distal radio-ulnar joints with the interosseous membrane between them. The radial head spins inside the annular ligament while the distal radius sweeps around the ulnar head.

Because the two bones must stay the right distance apart to do this, a fracture of one with dislocation of the other joint is a recognised pair: Monteggia (proximal ulna fracture with radial head dislocation) and Galeazzi (distal radius fracture with distal radio-ulnar dislocation). Always x-ray the joint above and below.
steps.mnemonic: MUGR: Monteggia = Ulna fracture; Galeazzi = Radius fracture.

check.q: A child has a fractured proximal ulna. Which joint must you check on the film?
check.a: The radiocapitellar joint — a Monteggia injury dislocates the radial head.

steps.title: The sheet between the bones carries force
steps.text:
Most load arriving from the carpus first enters the radius. The interosseous membrane does more than keep two bones apart: its strong central fibres run obliquely from the radius towards the ulna, allowing part of that load to be transferred to the ulna on its way to the elbow.

Think of the forearm as a linked unit with a joint at either end and a tensioned sheet between them. Damage to that sheet can allow the radius to migrate proximally, especially if the radial head is also damaged. The geometry needed for pronation and supination depends on the whole unit remaining aligned.

check.q: Why can damage at the radial head be associated with a problem at the wrist?
check.a: The radius, ulna, interosseous membrane and both radioulnar joints form one linked mechanical unit; loss of longitudinal stability can affect both ends.

title: The carpus and the skeleton of the hand
summary: Eight small bones in two rows, one of which dies if you get it wrong.
objectives: Name the eight carpal bones in order in both rows
Explain why the scaphoid is prone to avascular necrosis
Describe the arches of the hand and what flattens them
Relate the first carpometacarpal joint to opposition and precision grip
takeaways: Proximal row lateral to medial: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.
Distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.
Scaphoid blood supply enters distally, so proximal pole fractures may never heal.
Opposition combines movement and rotation at the first carpometacarpal joint so the thumb pad faces a fingertip.

steps.title: Two rows of four
steps.text:
From thumb to little finger, the proximal row is scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; the distal row is trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate. Learn them in that order and never in any other.

The proximal row has no tendon attached to it except through the pisiform: it is an intercalated segment, a set of free-floating bones whose position is decided entirely by the shape of its neighbours and the ligaments between them. That is why ligament injuries here produce lasting deformity.
steps.mnemonic: Some Lovers Try Positions That They Cannot Handle.

check.q: Name the distal row from lateral to medial.
check.a: Trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate.

steps.title: The scaphoid
steps.text:
The scaphoid bridges both rows, which makes it the mechanical link of the wrist and the bone that fails when you fall on an outstretched hand. It is tender in the anatomical snuffbox, between the tendons of extensor pollicis longus and brevis.

Its blood supply enters through the distal pole and runs backwards. Break the waist or the proximal pole and you cut the supply to the proximal fragment: avascular necrosis and non-union follow. That is why a snuffbox-tender wrist is immobilised and re-imaged even when the first film is normal.
steps.clinical: A missed scaphoid fracture ends in a painful arthritic wrist in a young adult. Treat the clinical picture, not the first radiograph.

check.q: Why does a proximal pole scaphoid fracture so often fail to unite?
check.a: The blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so the proximal fragment is left avascular.

steps.title: The lunate and the two dislocations
steps.text:
The lunate sits in the middle of the proximal row, articulating with the radius above. It is the bone that dislocates: in a lunate dislocation the lunate is pushed forwards out of line while the rest of the carpus stays put; in a perilunate dislocation the lunate stays with the radius and the rest of the carpus goes backwards.

Either way the displaced bone sits in the carpal tunnel and compresses the median nerve. On a lateral radiograph, radius, lunate and capitate should line up like three links of a chain — if they do not, look harder.

steps.title: The carpal tunnel floor and the hook of the hamate
steps.text:
The carpal bones are not flat: they form a deep gutter, concave forwards, roofed by the flexor retinaculum to make the carpal tunnel. The four corners of that roof are the scaphoid tubercle and trapezium on the radial side, and the pisiform and hook of the hamate on the ulnar side.

The hook is broken by racquet and club sports and by a fall onto the heel of the hand, and because the ulnar nerve and artery pass just lateral to it in Guyon's canal, the fracture presents with ulnar-sided numbness rather than a fracture pain.

check.q: Which nerve is at risk from a fractured hook of hamate?
check.a: The ulnar nerve, in Guyon's canal.

steps.title: Metacarpals, phalanges and the arches
steps.text:
Five metacarpals, then three phalanges for each finger and two for the thumb. The thumb's carpometacarpal joint is a saddle joint on the trapezium, and it is the reason the thumb can oppose — and the joint that wears out first, giving the squared-off thumb base of basal thumb arthritis.

The hand holds two arches: a fixed transverse arch at the distal carpal row, and a mobile one at the metacarpal heads. Flatten them — by swelling, scarring or intrinsic muscle paralysis — and grip is lost even with normal tendons. It is why a hand is splinted in the 'safe position', with the knuckles flexed.

check.q: Which joint gives the thumb its opposition, and what kind of joint is it?
check.a: The first carpometacarpal joint, a saddle joint between trapezium and first metacarpal.

steps.title: Opposition is more than bending the thumb
steps.text:
Find the base of the first metacarpal. Its joint with the trapezium has saddle-shaped surfaces that allow movement in two main planes. As the thumb moves across the palm, accompanying rotation turns its pad towards the pads of the fingers. That combination is opposition.

Flexing only the thumb's interphalangeal joint bends its tip without creating the same pad-to-pad contact. In precision grip, the mobile first ray meets fingers supported by the comparatively firm second and third carpometacarpal joints. The more mobile fourth and fifth rays help the palm cup round a larger object.

check.q: Why does bending the tip of the thumb alone fail to demonstrate true opposition?
check.a: Opposition requires movement and rotation of the first metacarpal so the thumb pad turns towards the fingers; interphalangeal flexion alone only bends the tip.

title: The bony pelvis
summary: Three bones fused into one, a ring that cannot break once, and the differences that matter in labour.
objectives: Identify ilium, ischium and pubis and the acetabulum they share
Distinguish the greater and lesser pelvis and the pelvic brim
List the features that distinguish a female from a male pelvis
Explain how the sacrum transfers trunk weight into the two hip bones
takeaways: The three bones meet in the acetabulum at a Y-shaped triradiate cartilage that fuses in the teens.
The pelvis is a ring: a displaced fracture in one place means a second break or a joint disruption somewhere else.
A female pelvis is wider and shallower with a rounder inlet and a subpubic angle over 80°.
Load passes from L5 to the sacrum, across the sacro-iliac joints and into the acetabula; posterior ligaments resist sacral tilt.

steps.title: Three bones, one socket
steps.text:
Each hip bone is three bones fused: the ilium above, the ischium behind and below, and the pubis in front. They meet in the acetabulum at a Y-shaped triradiate cartilage, which fuses between 16 and 18 — and which, in a child, can be mistaken for a fracture on a radiograph.

The two hip bones meet in front at the pubic symphysis and behind at the sacro-iliac joints, making a complete bony ring.

check.q: Which three bones meet in the acetabulum?
check.a: Ilium, ischium and pubis.

steps.title: A ring cannot break once
steps.text:
Because the pelvis is a closed ring of bone and strong ligaments, a single displaced break is mechanically impossible: if one part of the ring has moved, something else has given way too. Find the second injury.

The ring is held by the posterior sacro-iliac ligaments — the strongest in the body — with the sacrospinous and sacrotuberous ligaments resisting the tilt of the sacrum. Disruption behind is what makes a pelvic fracture bleed: the presacral venous plexus and the internal iliac branches tear with it.
steps.clinical: A pelvic binder at the level of the greater trochanters closes an open-book fracture and reduces the volume the pelvis can bleed into.

steps.title: Greater and lesser pelvis
steps.text:
The pelvic brim — sacral promontory, arcuate line, pectineal line, pubic crest — divides the greater (false) pelvis above, which is really part of the abdominal cavity and holds ileum and sigmoid, from the lesser (true) pelvis below, which holds the bladder, rectum and reproductive organs.

The lesser pelvis has an inlet at the brim and an outlet bounded by the pubic arch, the ischial tuberosities, the sacrotuberous ligaments and the coccyx. In labour, the head must negotiate both, and their shapes differ by 90°: the inlet is widest transversely, the outlet widest anteroposteriorly. That is why the head rotates on the way through.

check.q: Why must the fetal head rotate during descent?
check.a: The inlet is widest side to side and the outlet widest front to back.

steps.title: Male and female
steps.text:
The female pelvis is built to let a head through and the male pelvis to carry weight. Female: a rounder, wider inlet; a shallower cavity with straighter walls; a wider subpubic angle (over 80°, roughly your thumb and index finger spread); more everted ischial tuberosities; a shorter, broader, flatter sacrum.

Male: a heart-shaped inlet, a narrow deep cavity, a subpubic angle around 60°, and heavier bone with more prominent muscle markings.

check.q: Which single measurement best separates the sexes on a dry pelvis?
check.a: The subpubic angle — over about 80° in the female, around 60° in the male.

steps.title: The landmarks you can feel
steps.text:
Six to find on yourself. The iliac crest ends in front at the anterior superior iliac spine — origin of sartorius and the inguinal ligament — and behind at the posterior superior iliac spine, marked by a skin dimple over the S2 level.

The pubic tubercle is the medial attachment of the inguinal ligament and the reference point for telling an inguinal from a femoral hernia. The ischial tuberosity is what you sit on and the origin of the hamstrings. The highest point of the iliac crest is level with L4, which is how you find the space for a lumbar puncture.

check.q: The highest point of the iliac crest lies at which vertebral level?
check.a: L4 — Tuffier's line, used to find the L3/4 or L4/5 interspace.

steps.title: The route from the spine to the legs
steps.text:
Start at L5 and trace body weight down into the sacrum, across the two sacro-iliac joints and along the hip bones to the acetabula. When standing, the femoral heads receive that load. When sitting, much of the support instead passes towards the ischial tuberosities.

The sacrum tends to tilt under load, with its upper part moving forwards. The interosseous and posterior sacro-iliac ligaments, helped by the sacrotuberous and sacrospinous ligaments, resist this movement. Stability depends on both the shape of the joint surfaces and their ligamentous ties; a bony ring alone is not the whole explanation.

check.q: Which two bony contact regions take much of the load when you change from standing to sitting?
check.a: Standing transmits load towards the acetabula and femoral heads; sitting transfers much of it to the ischial tuberosities.

title: Femur, tibia and fibula
summary: The longest bone in the body, a strut that carries almost nothing, and the angles that decide how you walk.
objectives: Name the parts of the femur and describe its blood supply
Explain why an intracapsular hip fracture is treated differently from an extracapsular one
Say what the fibula is actually for
Distinguish the mechanical axis of the lower limb from the anatomical axis of the femoral shaft
takeaways: The femoral head is supplied mainly by retinacular vessels running up the neck, so an intracapsular fracture threatens it.
The tibia carries about five sixths of the load; the fibula carries the rest and provides muscle attachment and the lateral malleolus.
The subcutaneous anteromedial surface of the tibia is why tibial fractures are so often open.
The mechanical axis links hip, knee and ankle centres; it differs from the oblique anatomical axis of the femur.

steps.title: The femur
steps.text:
The longest and strongest bone in the body. A rounded head with a central pit (the fovea) for the ligament of the head; a neck angled about 125° from the shaft; the greater and lesser trochanters; a shaft bowed slightly forwards; and two condyles below.

Because the head is offset from the shaft, body weight puts a bending force across the neck. That is why the neck is the part that fails in an elderly osteoporotic fall, and why the trabeculae inside it are arranged along the lines of stress.

check.q: What is the normal angle between the neck and the shaft of the femur?
check.a: About 125° in an adult — larger (coxa valga) or smaller (coxa vara) changes the mechanics of the hip.

steps.title: The blood supply of the head, and why the fracture line matters
steps.text:
Three sources feed the femoral head: retinacular vessels from the medial and lateral circumflex femoral arteries, running up the neck under the capsular reflection; a small artery in the ligament of the head, which matters in childhood and little afterwards; and nutrient vessels up the shaft.

So a fracture inside the capsule tears the retinacular vessels and risks avascular necrosis: in an older patient it is replaced. A fracture outside the capsule, between the trochanters, leaves the supply intact and is fixed with a screw and plate.
steps.clinical: A shortened, externally rotated leg after a fall is a fractured neck of femur until proved otherwise.

check.q: Which artery supplies most of the adult femoral head?
check.a: The medial circumflex femoral, through the retinacular vessels along the neck.

steps.title: The tibia
steps.text:
The weight-bearing bone of the leg. Its expanded upper end carries the medial and lateral condyles with the intercondylar eminence between them, and in front the tibial tuberosity, where the patellar tendon inserts.

Its anteromedial surface is subcutaneous from top to bottom — feel it now — which explains two things: tibial fractures are often open, and the shin is a favourite site for a bone graft or an intraosseous line.

steps.title: The fibula, which carries almost nothing
steps.text:
The fibula transmits about a sixth of the load. Its real jobs are to give muscles somewhere to attach, to form the lateral malleolus and so the outer wall of the ankle mortise, and to anchor the interosseous membrane.

That is why a length of fibula can be harvested as a vascularised bone graft, and why an isolated fibular shaft fracture with an intact mortise can be treated in a boot. The common fibular nerve winds round its neck, subcutaneously: a plaster edge, a tight bandage or a fracture there gives foot drop.

check.q: Where is the common fibular nerve most vulnerable, and what does its injury cause?
check.a: At the neck of the fibula; injury causes foot drop and numbness of the dorsum of the foot.

steps.title: Angles, and how they change with age
steps.text:
The femur runs obliquely from a wide pelvis to a knee under the centre of gravity, so the femoral shaft and tibia meet at a slight valgus. Exaggerate it and you have knock knee (genu valgum); reverse it and you have bow leg (genu varum).

Children are normally bow-legged until about two, knock-kneed from three to five, and straight by seven. Knowing that saves a great deal of unnecessary worry — and makes the pathological ones, which are asymmetrical, painful or progressive, stand out.

check.q: A three-year-old is knock-kneed. Is this normal?
check.a: Yes — physiological genu valgum peaks at 3 to 5 years and corrects by about 7.

steps.title: A shaft line and a weight-bearing line
steps.text:
Draw an imaginary line down the centre of the femoral shaft: that is its anatomical axis. Now connect the centre of the femoral head to the centre of the knee. That is the femur's mechanical axis. They differ because the head sits medial to the shaft on an angled neck.

Extend the weight-bearing line towards the centre of the ankle. In a normally aligned limb it passes near the centre of the knee, although alignment varies between people. A varus alignment shifts loading towards the medial knee compartment; valgus shifts it laterally. Bone angles matter because they change where a joint carries force.

check.q: Why is the femoral shaft axis different from its mechanical axis?
check.a: The femoral head is offset medially from the shaft by the femoral neck, so a hip-to-knee line is not parallel to the shaft.

title: The skeleton of the foot and its arches
summary: Twenty-six bones arranged as three arches, held up by ligament first and muscle second.
objectives: Name the seven tarsal bones and their arrangement
Describe the medial, lateral and transverse arches and what supports each
Explain the significance of the fifth metatarsal base and the talar neck
Locate the second metatarsal base within the stable tarsometatarsal arrangement
takeaways: Talus, calcaneus, navicular, cuboid and three cuneiforms.
The spring ligament and the plantar fascia hold the medial arch up; muscles only help.
No muscle attaches to the talus, and its blood supply is retrograde — hence avascular necrosis after talar neck fracture.
The recessed second metatarsal base helps stabilise the midfoot; the Lisfranc ligament links the medial cuneiform to that base.

steps.title: The seven tarsals
steps.text:
Behind: the talus above the calcaneus. In front of them, the navicular on the medial side and the cuboid on the lateral, then the three cuneiforms in a row.

The tarsals bear weight the way carpals never do, so they are chunky and locked together by short strong ligaments. The foot is a platform first and a manipulator a long way second.

check.q: Which tarsal bone lies directly under the tibia?
check.a: The talus.

steps.title: The talus takes the load and pays for it
steps.text:
The talus transmits the whole body weight from the tibia to the foot, and it does so with no muscle attached to it anywhere — it is held entirely by ligaments and by the shape of the mortise.

Its blood supply enters mostly through the neck and runs backwards into the body. Fracture the neck and the body loses its supply: avascular necrosis follows in a high proportion of displaced fractures.
steps.clinical: A talar neck fracture is a high-energy injury — the classic 'aviator's astragalus' from a foot forced upwards on a rudder pedal.

steps.title: The calcaneus and Böhler's angle
steps.text:
The calcaneus is the heel and the longest bone of the foot. Its posterior tuberosity takes the Achilles tendon; the sustentaculum tali juts medially to hold up the talus, with flexor hallucis longus grooving its underside.

A fall from a height drives the talus into it and crushes it. The flattening is measured as Böhler's angle, normally 20–40°. Because both heels usually land, look at the other foot too — and at the lumbar spine, which is fractured in about 10% of them.

check.q: A man jumps from a wall and both heels hurt. What else must you image?
check.a: The lumbar spine — axial loading fractures accompany calcaneal fractures in about one in ten.

steps.title: The metatarsals, and the fifth base
steps.text:
Five metatarsals, with the first short and thick for weight and the second locked deep between the cuneiforms — which is why the second is the one that suffers a march fracture in a route march or a new runner.

The base of the fifth metatarsal takes the tendon of fibularis brevis and is avulsed in an inversion injury. Do not confuse the transverse avulsion fracture with the normal longitudinal apophysis in a child, and do not confuse either with a Jones fracture a couple of centimetres distal, which sits in a watershed of blood supply and often fails to unite.
steps.pitfall: An apophysis runs parallel to the shaft; an avulsion fracture runs across it.

steps.title: Three arches
steps.text:
The medial longitudinal arch — calcaneus, talus, navicular, cuneiforms, first three metatarsals — is the high, springy one. The lateral longitudinal arch is low and almost flat on the ground. The transverse arch runs across the cuneiforms and cuboid.

What holds them up, in order of importance: the shape of the bones, then the plantar ligaments — above all the spring (plantar calcaneonavicular) ligament under the head of the talus — then the plantar aponeurosis, and only then muscle. Tibialis posterior is the main muscular support of the medial arch, and its failure in middle age is the usual cause of an acquired flat foot.

check.q: Which ligament is the keystone support of the medial longitudinal arch?
check.a: The plantar calcaneonavicular (spring) ligament.

steps.title: The windlass
steps.text:
Stand up and push off. As the toes extend at the metatarsophalangeal joints, the plantar aponeurosis — anchored to the calcaneus behind and the toes in front — is wound round the metatarsal heads like a rope round a windlass. It shortens, the arch rises, and the foot converts from a shock absorber into a rigid lever.

The same mechanism explains plantar fasciitis pain: worst on the first steps in the morning, when the fascia is tightened suddenly after a night of shortening.

check.q: Why does the arch rise as you go up on your toes?
check.a: The windlass mechanism — extending the toes winds the plantar aponeurosis round the metatarsal heads and shortens it.

steps.title: The second ray is tucked into a socket
steps.text:
The base of the second metatarsal sits farther back than its neighbours, recessed between the cuneiforms. This arrangement gives the tarsometatarsal region a firm central anchor while the more lateral rays retain enough movement to accommodate uneven ground.

The Lisfranc ligament links the medial cuneiform to the second metatarsal base. It helps bind the first and second rays together where there is no strong direct intermetatarsal ligament between their bases. Disruption can separate the rays and destabilise the midfoot even when no large bone fragment is displaced.

check.q: Which two bones are linked by the Lisfranc ligament?
check.a: The medial cuneiform and the base of the second metatarsal.

steps.pitfall: A stable-looking arch from the side does not by itself prove that the tarsometatarsal ligaments are intact.

title: How a long bone is built
summary: Cortex, cancellous bone, marrow and a growth plate — and what each one means on a radiograph.
objectives: Name the regions of a growing long bone
Relate compact and cancellous bone to the forces each carries
Explain why a fracture through the physis is classified separately
Describe the sequence of secondary fracture healing from haematoma to remodelling
takeaways: Diaphysis, metaphysis, physis, epiphysis — from the middle out.
Compact bone is built of osteons around central canals; cancellous bone is trabeculae aligned along stress.
Bone is remodelled continuously by osteoblasts and osteoclasts, which is why it adapts to load and heals without a scar.
Secondary healing proceeds through haematoma, soft callus, hard callus and remodelling; the early callus is not mature lamellar bone.

steps.title: The regions of a growing bone
steps.text:
From the middle out: the diaphysis is the shaft, a thick-walled tube of compact bone round a marrow cavity. It flares at each end into the metaphysis, filled with cancellous bone. Between metaphysis and epiphysis sits the physis, the growth plate, a disc of cartilage that keeps making bone until it fuses.

The epiphysis carries the joint surface, capped with hyaline articular cartilage. The whole bone except that cartilage is wrapped in periosteum, which is where the pain, the blood supply and much of the healing come from.

check.q: Which layer makes bone hurt when it is bruised?
check.a: The periosteum — it is richly innervated; the bone within is not.

steps.title: Compact and cancellous
steps.text:
Compact (cortical) bone is dense and takes bending and torsion. Its unit is the osteon: concentric lamellae round a central canal carrying a vessel and a nerve, with osteocytes trapped in lacunae between them, talking to one another through canaliculi.

Cancellous (trabecular) bone is a lattice. Its struts line up along the principal stresses — clearest in the neck of the femur, where you can read the compressive and tensile trabecular groups off a radiograph. Lose them, as in osteoporosis, and the neck fails.

steps.title: Marrow
steps.text:
The cavity is not empty. Red marrow makes blood; yellow marrow is fat. A newborn has red marrow throughout; with age it retreats to the axial skeleton and the proximal ends of the femur and humerus — which is where a marrow biopsy is taken from, usually the posterior iliac crest.

Under stress, such as chronic anaemia, yellow marrow can turn red again, and the expanded marrow can visibly thin the cortex.

steps.title: The growth plate, and why it is a special case
steps.text:
The physis is the weakest part of a child's skeleton — weaker than the ligaments around it. So the injury that sprains an adult's ankle fractures a child's growth plate.

The Salter-Harris classification runs from I (through the plate alone) to V (a crush), and the higher grades cross into the joint surface or the metaphysis and threaten growth arrest. A bar of bone across part of the plate makes the limb grow crooked, which is why these injuries are followed up long after they have healed.
steps.mnemonic: SALTR: Slipped, Above, Lower, Through, Rammed — types I to V.

check.q: Why does a child sprain a growth plate where an adult tears a ligament?
check.a: The physis is weaker than the surrounding ligaments until it fuses.

steps.title: Bone is never finished
steps.text:
Osteoblasts lay bone down, osteoclasts take it away, and osteocytes — former osteoblasts walled into the matrix — sense strain and decide where the work happens. About 10% of the adult skeleton is replaced each year.

Two consequences. Loaded bone thickens and unloaded bone thins, which is why immobility and weightlessness cause bone loss and why weight-bearing exercise protects against osteoporosis. And a fracture heals by rebuilding real bone rather than scar, so a well-remodelled childhood fracture eventually becomes invisible.

check.q: Which cell senses mechanical strain in bone?
check.a: The osteocyte, from within the matrix.

steps.title: How the gap becomes bone again
steps.text:
In secondary fracture healing, torn vessels first produce a haematoma and an inflammatory response. Repair tissue then bridges the gap as a soft callus containing fibrous tissue and cartilage. This early bridge limits movement but does not yet have the strength of normal bone.

New woven bone replaces the soft callus to form a hard callus. Remodelling then reshapes that bridge into organised lamellar bone and restores the marrow cavity as loading allows. The stages overlap, and healing depends on blood supply and mechanical conditions. Bone repair is a changing tissue process, not simply glue filling a crack.

check.q: Why is a soft callus not the same as a healed, fully strong bone?
check.a: It is an early fibrous and cartilaginous bridge that still has to be replaced by bone and remodelled.

steps.pitfall: Rigidly stabilised fractures can heal directly with little visible callus; the callus sequence describes secondary healing.
